messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Mrs. Le Thi is a 74-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who presents with significant symptoms following her child’s life-threatening illness five years ago. Mrs. Le Thi has been married for over fifty years and works as a software engineer at a tech company in California. The traumatic event occurred when her youngest daughter, then only eight years old, fell into a severe case of pneumonia that required multiple hospitalizations and intensive care. The hospitalization was prolonged, and the silence during those long nights was suffocating; every whisper of machinery and the occasional beep of monitors punctuated the stillness with an eerie quietude. Mrs. Le Thi remembers feeling as though the silence itself was a prelude to some further calamity, making her heart race and her skin crawl. Since then, sudden or complete silence has become a potent trigger for her, evoking vivid flashbacks of those long nights in the hospital. One particular instance stands out when she came home from work one evening and found the house unusually quiet—her husband was on a trip and their daughter had gone to a friend’s place. The profound silence instantly transported her back to that hospital room, and she experienced a surge of terror, her heart pounding with anxiety. The antiseptic smell of hospitals also triggers intense recollections for Mrs. Le Thi. Recently, when she visited her husband for his routine check-up at the clinic, the familiar scent overwhelmed her, bringing back waves of shame and helplessness. She had come to believe that the world is an inherently dangerous place, and her inability to protect her daughter from illness has led her to feel deeply responsible for what happened. Her hypervigilance extends beyond these specific triggers into her daily life. At work, she finds herself constantly on edge, especially when cars drive past the building where she works. The sound of car horns and engine revving often remind her of that fateful day when they rushed to the hospital in a panic. This hyperalertness has started affecting her focus at work; several times, she has missed important deadlines because she was preoccupied with monitoring potential threats. Mrs. Le Thi’s difficulty falling asleep is another manifestation of this hypervigilance. Each night, as she lies in bed, her mind races through worst-case scenarios, and the need to stay alert keeps her awake. She often spends hours staring at the ceiling, trying to calm herself by focusing on deep breathing exercises. The memory of those nights in the hospital is fragmented yet potent. Sometimes, when she closes her eyes, all she feels is the overwhelming terror and shame without any clear image, as though the emotion itself is enough to engulf her. She has become acutely aware that even small reminders can set off these intense emotional reactions, leading her to avoid certain environments and situations. This avoidance has had real consequences in her life. Her marriage has been strained because she often cancels plans or refuses to go out due to fear of encountering a trigger. At work, her colleagues have noticed a decline in her productivity and occasional absences, which have led to some tensions with her supervisors. What finally brought Mrs. Le Thi to seek help was the realization that these symptoms were escalating and affecting every aspect of her life. She is most afraid of losing control and becoming unable to function normally. However, she also harbors a glimmer of hope—that through therapy, she might be able to regain some semblance of normalcy and find peace with her past experiences.
